questions.question: A 58-year-old man has a 3 cm biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal with a palpable inguinal node. Staging CT shows no distant disease. What is the best initial treatment?

options.A: Abdominoperineal resection with inguinal node dissection
options.C: Wide local excision followed by radiation
options.D: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by abdominoperineal resection

questions.explanation: Chemoradiation (Nigro protocol: 5-FU, mitomycin C, and radiation including the inguinal nodes) is first-line for anal canal SCC, even with nodal disease, and preserves the sphincter in most patients. Don't treat it like rectal adenocarcinoma: APR is reserved for persistent or recurrent disease after chemoradiation, not planned after neoadjuvant therapy.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has 2 years of progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, and 8-kg weight loss. Her barium swallow is shown in the image. EGD shows no mucosal lesion or mass. Which study best confirms the diagnosis?

options.C: CT scan of the chest and abdomen

questions.explanation: The image shows a dilated esophagus with smooth bird's beak tapering at the GE junction, typical of achalasia. With malignancy excluded by EGD, high-resolution manometry is the gold standard. It shows incomplete LES relaxation (elevated IRP) and absent peristalsis, and its subtype guides therapy. pH monitoring evaluates GERD and does not diagnose achalasia. CT is only used if EGD raises concern for pseudoachalasia.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man has a 3 cm liver lesion found on CT for flank pain. MRI with hepatobiliary contrast is consistent with hepatocellular adenoma. He uses anabolic steroids and agrees to stop. What is the best management?
questions.explanation: Resect hepatocellular adenomas in men at any size because their risk of malignant transformation is much higher. Stopping hormones and reimaging is appropriate for women with adenomas under 5 cm, not for men. Biopsy carries bleeding risk and won't change management here. Embolization is mainly used to control acute hemorrhage.

questions.question: A 1-day-old with Down syndrome has bilious emesis after first feeds. The abdomen is soft and nondistended. An abdominal radiograph is shown in the image. What is the best next step in management?

options.A: Emergent upper GI contrast study to exclude malrotation with volvulus
options.B: Gastric decompression, IV fluids, echocardiogram, then duodenoduodenostomy
options.D: Contrast enema to evaluate for microcolon

questions.explanation: The image shows a double bubble: a dilated stomach and proximal duodenum with no distal bowel gas, diagnostic of duodenal atresia. No further imaging is needed. Management is gastric decompression, fluid resuscitation, and screening for associated anomalies, especially cardiac, followed by duodenoduodenostomy. An upper GI study is reserved for cases with distal gas, where malrotation with volvulus must be excluded.
questions.image_credit: Image: Kinderradiologie Olgahospital Klinikum S, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

questions.question: A new colorectal cancer screening test validated in a high-risk referral clinic is applied to the general population, where disease prevalence is much lower. Which change in test performance is expected?

options.A: PPV decreases; sensitivity and specificity are unchanged

questions.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic to the test and don't change with prevalence. Predictive values do change. At lower prevalence, more positives are false positives, so PPV falls, while NPV rises. That is why both values can't fall together, and why screening low-prevalence populations generates many false positives.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with severe gallstone pancreatitis is intubated on hospital day 3. Echo shows normal LV function. On 6 mL/kg IBW tidal volume, FiO2 0.8, and PEEP 14, PaO2 is 64 mmHg. Based on the image, what is the best next step?

options.A: Prone positioning for at least 16 hours per day

questions.explanation: The image shows bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates. With normal LV function and P/F 80, this is severe ARDS. Once low tidal volume ventilation and adequate PEEP are in place, early prone positioning for at least 16 h/day reduces mortality when P/F is below 150 (PROSEVA). VV-ECMO is a rescue therapy for refractory hypoxemia after proning fails. Inhaled NO improves oxygenation without a survival benefit. Diuresis does not treat non-cardiogenic edema.
questions.image_credit: Image: Samir, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

questions.question: An unconscious 45-year-old man arrives after a motorcycle crash with BP 70/40 and a positive FAST. No family, surrogate, or advance directive can be found. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Delay surgery until next of kin can be reached
options.B: Obtain an emergency court order before operating
options.C: Proceed with laparotomy under implied consent
options.D: Request an ethics consultation before operating

questions.explanation: In a life-threatening emergency, when the patient lacks capacity and no surrogate or known wishes are available, the emergency exception lets you proceed. We presume a reasonable person would consent to lifesaving care. Waiting for a court order, an ethics consult, or family would cause harmful delay in a patient in hemorrhagic shock. Document the emergency and your reasoning.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with MEN2A has an elevated calcitonin, a 2 cm thyroid nodule, and a 4 cm adrenal mass with elevated plasma metanephrines. She has been alpha-blocked. What is the correct operative sequence?

options.A: Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection, then adrenalectomy
options.B: Adrenalectomy, then total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection
options.C: Simultaneous thyroidectomy and adrenalectomy without staging

questions.explanation: Always remove the pheochromocytoma first, after alpha blockade. Operating on the thyroid with an untreated pheo risks a fatal hypertensive crisis. Then perform total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection for medullary thyroid cancer. Surveillance alone isn't acceptable because MTC in MEN2A is the main determinant of survival.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman with dyspepsia has EGD biopsies showing low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma confined to the mucosa and submucosa. H. pylori testing is positive. What is the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Early-stage low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma is driven by H. pylori, and eradication alone produces remission in most patients. Confirm eradication and follow with surveillance endoscopy. Radiation is used for persistent disease or H. pylori-negative tumors. Gastrectomy no longer has a routine role, and chemotherapy is for high-grade or advanced disease.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man is 4 weeks into severe gallstone pancreatitis and has new fever and rising WBC. CT shows a walled-off necrotic collection containing gas. He is stable on antibiotics. What is the next step?

options.C: CT-guided fine-needle aspiration for Gram stain and culture

questions.explanation: Gas in walled-off necrosis with clinical deterioration indicates infected necrosis. Use the step-up approach: start with endoscopic or percutaneous drainage, then escalate to minimally invasive necrosectomy if needed. Open necrosectomy has higher morbidity. FNA isn't needed when gas is present. Delay cholecystectomy until the collection resolves.

questions.question: Minutes after reperfusion of a renal allograft, the kidney becomes mottled, cyanotic, and flaccid. What is the underlying mechanism?

options.C: De novo donor-specific antibodies forming over weeks

questions.explanation: This is hyperacute rejection. Preformed antibodies against ABO or HLA antigens bind graft endothelium, activate complement, and cause immediate thrombosis. It is prevented by ABO matching and a negative crossmatch, and the graft must be removed. Acute cellular rejection is T-cell mediated and occurs days to months later.

questions.question: An 84-year-old woman is agitated and inattentive on POD 2 after hip fracture repair. Exam, labs, and urinalysis are unremarkable, and her pain is controlled. She is not endangering herself or staff. What is the best initial management?

options.A: Reorientation, sleep hygiene, glasses/hearing aids, early mobilization

questions.explanation: After you exclude reversible causes, manage delirium first with nonpharmacologic measures: reorientation, a normal sleep-wake cycle, sensory aids, mobilization, and removing tethers. Benzodiazepines worsen delirium in older adults and should be avoided. Restraints increase agitation and injury. Reserve antipsychotics for patients who are a danger to themselves or others.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man with perforated diverticulitis has a MAP of 56 and lactate of 4.2 despite 30 mL/kg crystalloid and broad-spectrum antibiotics. What is the next step in hemodynamic management?
questions.explanation: Surviving Sepsis guidelines make norepinephrine the first-line vasopressor for septic shock that persists after initial fluid resuscitation, targeting MAP 65 or higher. Dopamine causes more arrhythmias and is no longer favored. Add hydrocortisone only for ongoing vasopressor requirement. Give further fluid only if he is fluid-responsive. Arrange urgent source control.
